intro.html: Some thinking goes all the way down; some barely skims the surface. And some knowledge is so deep, or so specialized, that only a few people ever reach it. This topic gives you words for all three.

Deep or shallow: profound, superficial. Ways of thinking: cerebral (by the mind, not feelings), contemplate, ruminate (chew it over), pensive (quietly thoughtful). Knowledge few people share: abstruse, esoteric, arcane, recondite.

The four hard-knowledge words overlap, but each has its own picture: abstruse is pushed away out of reach, esoteric is for the inner circle, arcane is locked in a chest, and recondite is hidden away at the back.

words.def: very deep in thought, feeling or effect
words.ex: Grandma’s quiet advice had a {profound} effect on how I treat my friends.
words.ctx: Though the child spoke in simple words, her answer was {profound}; the room fell silent as the grown-ups realized she had seen to the heart of the problem.
words.etym: From Latin profundus, “deep”: pro- (forward, down) + fundus (bottom).

mn.cue: PRO-FOUND: FOUND at the very bottom
mn.text: Professor Edwin climbs down to the deepest part of the cave and finds a glowing gem no one else ever reached; a thought that comes from that deep is {profound}.

labels.text: PRO-FOUND: FOUND at the DEEPEST bottom

scene.alt: An old professor with a lantern kneels deep in a cave beside a glowing gem.

words.def: on the surface only; not deep or thorough
words.ex: Luckily, the scratch on the car door was only {superficial}.
words.ctx: His knowledge of the subject was {superficial}: he could repeat a few famous names and dates, but he could not explain why any of it mattered.
words.etym: From Latin superficialis, from superficies (surface): super (above) + facies (face).

mn.text: The little fish skims the top of the sea all day and never looks below, missing the treasure on the bottom; its view of the sea is {superficial}.

scene.alt: A fish swims at the top of the water, never noticing the treasure chest on the sea floor below.

words.def: having to do with careful thinking rather than feelings
words.ex: Chess is a {cerebral} game, all planning and no luck.
words.ctx: Her brother loved action movies full of car chases, but Ada preferred {cerebral} films, where the excitement came from puzzles and clever conversation.

mn.text: While the other kids race around the field, Sami sits under a tree working out a chess puzzle; he likes the {cerebral} kind of fun.

scene.alt: A boy thinks hard over a chess piece while other children run and play in the background.

words.def: to think long and carefully about something, or to look at it thoughtfully
words.ex: Rosa sat on the dock to {contemplate} the sunset.
words.ctx: Before accepting the job overseas, Jamal took a week to {contemplate} the choice, weighing what he would gain against everything he would leave behind.

roots.means: an open space marked out for watching
to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin contemplari, “to observe carefully,” from templum, an open space marked out for watching the sky.

mn.cue: con-tem-PLATE: staring at the PLATE, thinking
mn.text: Dev stares at the last slice of pizza on the plate for a long time: eat it or save it for his sister? He {contemplates} the question.

scene.alt: A teen stares thoughtfully at the last slice of pizza on a plate, deciding whether to eat it.

words.def: quietly and deeply thoughtful, often a little sad
words.ex: On the last day of camp, the {pensive} campers watched the lake in silence.
words.ctx: Usually chatty at dinner, Grandpa was {pensive} that night, gazing out the window and answering every question with a faraway smile.
words.etym: From French pensif, from penser (to think), from Latin pensare (to weigh, to ponder).

mn.cue: PEN-SIVE: chewing the PEN, lost in thought
mn.text: Lila sits by the rainy window chewing on her pen, thinking about the friend who moved away; she is quiet and {pensive}.

scene.alt: A girl rests her chin on her hand, holding a pencil, lost in sad thought by the window.

words.def: to think something over again and again
words.ex: Kai lay awake, {ruminating} about the easy goal he had missed.
words.ctx: Rather than decide quickly, the judge preferred to {ruminate}, turning the case over in her mind for days before she wrote a single word.

roots.means: to make, to act on (in verbs)

words.etym: From Latin ruminari, “to chew the cud,” from rumen (throat).
words.note: Cows, sheep and goats are ruminants: they chew their food, swallow it and bring it back up to chew again.

mn.cue: a COW chewing it over and over
mn.text: Daisy the cow chews the same mouthful of grass for an hour, round and round; to chew a thought over like that is to {ruminate}.

scene.alt: A cow chews slowly with a thoughtful look, thinking something over.

words.ex: The professor’s {abstruse} lecture lost half the class in the first ten minutes.
words.ctx: The instruction manual was {abstruse}, full of technical terms and tangled diagrams that even the engineer struggled to follow.
words.etym: From Latin abstrusus, “hidden,” from abstrudere (to push away, to conceal): abs- (away) + trudere (to push).

mn.cue: AB-STRUSE: pushed AWAY out of reach
mn.text: Professor Edwin fills the board with symbols so tangled that every student’s head spins; the meaning is pushed far out of reach. His lecture is {abstruse}.

scene.alt: A professor points to a board of tangled symbols while a dizzy student cannot follow.

words.def: understood or enjoyed by only a small group
words.ex: The club’s {esoteric} jokes about antique buttons made no sense to newcomers.
words.ctx: Most visitors hurried past the exhibit, but a few experts lingered for hours; its subject, the history of buttons, was too {esoteric} for the general public.
words.etym: From Greek esoterikos, “belonging to an inner circle,” from a word meaning “within.”
words.note: Esoteric means for insiders, not simply strange. Its opposite is exoteric, meant for outsiders too.

mn.text: Inside the Button Club, three members laugh at a joke about four-hole buttons that no outsider understands; their humor is {esoteric}.

scene.alt: Three club members laugh at an inside joke while an outsider scratches his head.

words.def: known or understood by only a few; mysterious
words.ex: The old book was full of {arcane} rules for a card game no one plays anymore.
words.ctx: Only the oldest clerk understood the town’s {arcane} filing system, in which every folder was sorted by the color of its ink rather than by name or date.
words.etym: From Latin arcanus, “secret, hidden,” from arca (chest, box).

mn.text: The old wizard keeps his strangest spells locked in a chest, written in a script only he can read; they are {arcane}.

scene.alt: An old wizard reads a scroll beside a glowing chest of secret spells.

words.def: little known and hard to understand
words.ex: The quiz bowl team studied {recondite} facts about ancient coins and rare beetles.
words.ctx: Most readers found the essay {recondite}, packed with references to forgotten poets and obscure scientific papers that only a specialist would recognize.
words.etym: From Latin reconditus, “hidden away,” from recondere (to put away, to conceal).

mn.text: Ada climbs to the dustiest shelf at the back of the library for a book on the moths of a single mountain; knowledge hidden that far back is {recondite}.

scene.alt: A woman on a ladder reaches for a dusty book on the highest shelf at the back of a library.

picture inside
use it for
rows: pro + fundus: down to the bottom
after.cap: Deep, shallow and hidden: the pictures inside the words.

after.html: Three verbs and adjectives for thinking: to contemplate is to think long and carefully; to ruminate is to chew a thought over and over (like a cow with its cud); a pensive person is quietly, often sadly, thoughtful.

items.q: Which word also describes a cow chewing its cud?
items.why: Ruminate comes from Latin for chewing the cud: to ruminate on an idea is to chew it over and over.

items.q: “The lecture on medieval spoon-making was too esoteric for most of the audience.” Esoteric means…
choices: of interest only to a small, specialized group
items.why: Esoteric means understood or enjoyed by only a small circle of insiders.

items.q: Which word is the opposite of profound?
items.why: Profound means deep; superficial means on the surface only.

items.q: The Latin word arca, the root of arcane, means…
items.why: arca means a chest or box: arcane knowledge is locked away from most people.
